newsitem.title: USA: NYC mayor asks Albany for fair share of state aid.
newsitem.headline: NYC mayor asks Albany for fair share of state aid.

text.p: New York City Mayor Rudolph Giuliani Tuesday, promising Albany the city's "days of waste and profligate spending" were over, pressed lawmakers to give the city its fair share of aid, according to a draft text.

Giuliani, while complimenting Gov. George Patkai and the legislature for making sure the city boosted its police force, which has helped cut crime dramatically, urged them to correct disparities in the amount of money provided for property tax relief, schools and welform reform.

The Republican mayor, who spoke before the Joint Legislative Fiscal Committees, said he was willing to work with the City Council to freeze property tax rates to qualify for an ambitious, $3.4 billion, four-year plan to relieve property taxes that Pataki included in his fiscal 1998 budget.

However, Giuliani argued that the governor's plan should be modified as 80 percent of the city housing would not get any benefit because Pataki's program offers no relief to either renters or co-op owners. He added the tax plan penalized the city for its "tremendous success" in keeping property rates low and favored suburbanites.

The mayor estimated that when Pataki's tax plan is fully in place, homeowners in New York City only will get a tax break of $160 on average, a small share of the $1,130 that residents of Westchester County can expect to collect.

Giuliani, answering a lawmaker's question, said the city, which is owed about $700 million in receivables for school aid by the state, would need another $300 million to $500 million to correct the gap between its role in educating 37 percent of the state's children with only 34 percent of the aid. Instead of narrowing the gap, the fiscal 1998 budget will widen it by cutting the city's share to 34.65 percent from 34.84 percent.
"We contribute 46 percent of the state's revenues, and yet we will only receive nine percent of the tax relief under this proposal," he said, according to the draft text.

The mayor assured the lawmakers his Administration had corrected oversight problems that might have made Albany wary of trusting it with more money, and which last year led Giuliani to decline to promise to give the Board of Education, which now has a new chancellor, more state aid. "You should feel confident that your investment in the city will be used effectively and efficiently. The days of waste and profligate spending are over," he said.

Giuliani, who has become a national spokesman for legal immigrants, whose benefits were cut under the federal welfare changes that became law in August, called upon the Pataki Administration to use the same rules to decide if these residents get benefits as are used for citizens.

He estimated that the sweeping, new federal rules will cause New York, California, Florida and Texas to lose about 75 percent of the money Washington expects to save, and noted the city has 80 percent of the state's non-citizens.

City Council Speaker Peter Vallone, a Democrat, who also testified, faulted Pataki's proposed budget as it failed to give the city a fair share of the taxes it collected, and in an effort to close an estimated $3 billion budget gap, switched funds between programs in a harmful fashion.

"What the governor would give us in tax relief and increased education aid, he has paid for by shifting the cost of welfare reform to local taxpayers and by making bone-deep cuts in Medicaid," said Vallone, in prepared remarks.

The Speaker highlighted the Pataki Administration's decision not to seek a waiver from workfare requirements for the federal Food Stamps program unless an area has an unemployment rate of 10 percent or more, a decision he said will cause 75,000 people to lose benefits.
Allowing localities to keep up to 20 percent of what they save under the new welfare rules Pataki proposed would cause them to compete with each other to slash benefits, he said.

Noting how much of the city's revenues hinge on how well volatile Wall Street brokerage and banks perform, he said the biggest problem for the city was Pataki's plan to cap the Safety Net program for localities, which he said meant the city would assume all the risks of an economic downturn.

Vallone was skeptical of Patkai's promise to equalize school aid by 2002, calling it "the unreachable star," and blasted the governor's plan to slash spending on Medicaid, which pays for healthcare for the poor. Medicaid has been slashed two years in a row, and making the city pay 25 percent of the share Albany paid as "overburden aid" for acute care of the mentally diabled would cost it $45 million.
The Speaker called for a temporary, bipartisan Health Care Commission to evaluate the impact of deregulation on healthcare and report back to the legislature in January 1999.
